summary: Two chapters of a first complete draft, and the opening's problem is not craft but consequence: Chapter 1 builds real forward pressure and Chapter 2 spends it without replacing it. The chase works. What follows the chase does not yet exist as a scene, because the one live conflict — Mira paying for her passage with the ledger that condemns her uncle — keeps getting deferred, and Mira never registers that the payment is a betrayal. Three major findings (dev-001, dev-002, dev-003) are one connected repair plus one containable POV slip; the rest are moderate structural placement and a pair of local plot faults. Nothing here requires rebuilding the premise, which is fixed and working.
top_priorities: [dev-001] Chapter 2 honors none of Chapter 1's three live conditions — put a cost between the alley and the gangplank, and stop deferring the payment scene past the harbor mouth.

[dev-002] Mira never notices that her escape is purchased with her uncle's freedom — one beat of awareness behind the herring crate converts the ledger from fare to decision, and arms the scene dev-001 asks for.
[dev-003] Two lines at the gangplank hand the reader Renne's interior life, breaking the opacity you designed for; the same slip shows the camera stepping outside Mira twice.

[dev-004] The Chapter 2 history paragraph has three destinations: insurance clause into Chapter 1, Voss dramatized later in act one, town texture cut and seeded thinly — and the weld sentence deleted.
[dev-005] Mira's motivation is asserted, not grounded — nothing she's going toward, no trigger that makes tonight the night, no reason she chose her uncle.
[dev-006] The ledger's location contradicts itself within a page: paragraph 2 reads as customs having it, paragraph 4 as nobody having it, the plot as Mira carrying it.
[dev-007] Continuity: Mira's eyes are green in Chapter 1 and blue in Chapter 2.
developmental_notes:
The opening's engine is the chase, and the chase pays off. The problem is what happens after it. Chapter 1 sets three live conditions and Chapter 2 honors none of them (dev-001). Renne's passage is explicitly conditional — 'provided she brought something worth the risk' — but at the gangplank Renne never asks what Mira brought and boards her on credit. Chapter 1 ends with the alarm ringing and officers in the alleys; Chapter 2 opens on an empty dock at dawn with no pursuit, and the intervening hours compress into 'I had complications,' which means the only hard part of the night happens offstage. Then Renne defers the one live conflict past the chapter break: 'We'll talk about payment once we're clear of the harbor mouth.' A reader finishes Chapter 2 with less at risk than they had at the end of Chapter 1. The fix is two moves: put a cost between the alley and the gangplank — decide what 'complications' meant and what it took from her, an injury, a witness who saw her face, a lost hour that means the Gull is already casting off — and then play the payment scene on deck instead of promising it. Mira handing over the ledger in exchange for a berth is the scene Chapter 2 is circling.

That scene has no charge until dev-002 is fixed, which is why the two findings are really one repair. Chapter 1 states plainly that the ledger names every smuggler in Selkirk 'including her uncle,' and that if customs gets it 'half the harbor would be in chains by morning.' Chapter 1 also establishes that she intends to trade that exact object to Renne. Mira registers fear of being caught and never registers what she is about to do to him or to the harbor. The reader therefore cannot tell whether she is ruthless, desperate, or simply hasn't thought it through, and the ledger reads as a fare rather than as a betrayal she is carrying in her coat. One beat behind the herring crate does it — not remorse, just recognition of the trade and a reason she's making it anyway.

The POV work (dev-003) is a case of the prose contradicting your own design. You've decided Renne is opaque through act one, and two lines undo it: 'Renne had seen a hundred desperate people come aboard with a hundred desperate stories, and this one would be no different' is Renne's assessment from inside Renne's head, and 'something in her expression softened... in a way that suggested she recognized something of herself in this frightened, resourceful young woman' hands over her motive outright. Restrict both to what Mira can observe — the crossed arms, the pause, the tone of 'You're late' — and cut the softening, or keep only the physical change with no interpretation attached. This is a pattern rather than a one-off: the camera also steps outside Mira in 'her green eyes scanning the alleys' and 'Her blue eyes found the Gray Gull.' Mira does not see her own eyes, and she would not call herself 'resourceful.'

On placement of the Chapter 2 history material (dev-004): it wants three different homes. The insurance clause — that Mira's uncle kept the ledger precisely because the Voss family might come for him — is load-bearing plot; it sets the ledger's price and explains why anyone wants it. Move it up to Chapter 1, folded into the paragraph behind the herring crate where she's already thinking about what the ledger does. It's a line, not a paragraph. Halvard Voss is the only element in the passage that generates future pressure, and he's currently delivered as genealogy; he should arrive dramatized — a name spoken by a pursuing officer, a seal on a door, a man on the dock — somewhere in act one, not summarized before he's ever a threat. The 300-year founding, the Ashport wars, the forty-year-old customs office and its six chiefs are texture: cut them here, seed them thinly later in dialogue or in a detail Mira has reason to look at. The sentence holding the whole paragraph in place is 'Before she could board, she needed to understand everything that had led her here' — that invents a motive Mira does not have. She's fleeing, and she already knows her own town's history. Delete that sentence and the paragraph has nothing anchoring it.

Mira's motivation (dev-005) is asserted rather than grounded. 'Mira had always known she would leave the harbor town of Selkirk' is a claim the chapter never pays for: there's no sense of what Selkirk costs her or what she wants that isn't there, no reason it has to be tonight rather than any other night, and no reason she chose her own uncle as the mark. This is survivable for a page or two on pure adrenaline — the mid-chase opening is doing its job — but by the gangplank the reader still can't say what she wants beyond 'away.' One concrete detail apiece carries it: something specific she's going toward (a place, a person, a trade), and a trigger that made tonight the night. Make the trigger something the uncle did and you answer the why-him question in the same stroke.

Two local faults. The ledger's location is incoherent within a single page (dev-006): paragraph 2 says the alarm 'meant the customs officers had found the ledger she'd stolen from her uncle's shop,' which reads as customs having it; paragraph 4 says 'If the customs office got hold of it before she did, half the harbor would be in chains by morning,' which implies neither of them has it; and the plot requires her to be carrying it. A reader hits paragraph 4 and stops to re-litigate who's holding the book at the moment you most need them moving. Decide she has it, keep it physically present, and let the alarm mean customs discovered the theft rather than the object — the threat is that they take it off her body. And Mira's eyes are green in Chapter 1 and blue in Chapter 2 (dev-007); a straight fix, tracked separately from the POV note even though it cites the same two lines.
line_notes: Not covered: this is a developmental-phase letter; line editing comes after structure settles.
